tagline: Through Delaware, meetinghouses and a courthouse trace the struggle against slavery.
intro: The Delaware leg of the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway travels north through towns before following Route 9 along the Delaware River to Wilmington. DelDOT lists this Delaware Byway at approximately 95 miles with its loops and about three hours of driving. The agency presents it as an alternative route through the state, connecting places where Underground Railroad history happened.

Before the Civil War, freedom seekers traveled north through a network of people and landscapes known as the Underground Railroad. In Wilmington, Quaker Thomas Garrett organized members and safe locations. Harriet Tubman repeatedly passed through his station; he supplied lodging, meals, money and shoes for her journeys. In 1848, Garrett and fellow Quaker John Hunn were sued for helping the Hawkins family escape. Despite fines, both declared that they would continue their work; the New Castle courthouse joins meetinghouses and commemorative sites along the modern byway.

Begin where Maryland's byway ends, on Willow Grove Road in Kent County, then continue through Camden and Dover. US 13 leads through Smyrna, and Route 15 continues to Middletown and Odessa. Route 9 brings the journey to Wilmington and its 13 Underground Railroad sites before Kennett Pike carries the byway to the Pennsylvania line.

moments.title: Appoquinimink Friends Meetinghouse
moments.text: Measuring about 20 by 22 feet, the brick meetinghouse in Odessa connects Quaker worship with the Underground Railroad. Members John Hunn and John Alston took part in the network. Its basement and a loft with a removable panel under the eaves may have sheltered self-liberating Black people. After Alston, the last active member, died in 1874, the building deteriorated and was rented to farmers at different times. H. Rodney Sharp restored it in 1938, and worship resumed in 1939. Wilmington Monthly Meeting received title to the property in 2019. Quaker worship continues here.
moments.notice: The burial ground has early fieldstones as well as curved-top and modern markers.

moments.title: New Castle Court House
moments.text: In 1848, Thomas Garrett and John Hunn faced trial here for violating the Fugitive Slave Act. They had helped the family of Emeline and Samuel Hawkins escape slavery. Chief Justice Roger Taney presided, and both men were found guilty. Both received heavy fines, yet declared that they would continue helping people escape slavery. The courthouse also shaped a literal boundary: in 1750, a commission agreed to use its cupola as the center of the 12-mile circle. That circle defines most of the Delaware-Pennsylvania border. Delaware opened the courthouse as a museum in 1963.

moments.title: Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park
moments.text: Harriet Tubman, Thomas Garrett and two freedom seekers appear together in a bronze sculpture installed here in 2012. Mario Chiodo’s work is titled Unwavering Courage in the Pursuit of Freedom. The park honors Tubman and Garrett's work together as Underground Railroad operatives in the mid-19th century. Developed during Wilmington's riverfront revitalization in the late 1990s, the site provided public access to the Christina River. Across from the railroad station, it includes lawns, riverside walkways, historical markers and public art. The public park also serves as a venue for concerts, festivals and community events.
moments.notice: The bronze sculpture depicts Tubman, Garrett and two freedom seekers.
